x.name: alphaXiv
x.bio: High fidelity research

tweets.text:
“τ^τ-Bench: An Environment for End-To-End, Realistic Agent Construction”

Most agent benchmarks evaluate agents after they’re built. 

So τ^τ-Bench instead evaluates whether coding agents can build a deployable agent end-to-end from messy multimodal business records, client requirements, APIs, inherited code, and serving constraints.

The resulting agent is deployed against held-out simulated users, making the benchmark test specification recovery, agent design, and implementation rather than just coding.

The best system which is Claude Opus 5 + Claude Code, scores just 23.9% versus an 82.2% expert-authored ceiling, with most failures coming from shallow evidence search, barely questioning clients, and little architecture or cost optimization.

https://t.co/HHzi1AvJsX

“Continual Learning Mechanisms Compose for Long-Horizon Memorization”

catastrophically forgetting in sequential fine-tuning loses about 98.8% of knowledge after 100 tasks.

So this paper combines generative replay, self-distillation, weight regularization, and merged LoRA to preserve complementary forms of prior information.

Together, they were able to reach 34.9% final retention, with replay + merged LoRA showing super-additive benefits.

https://t.co/nsBxmXBHJG

“Don't Drop Dropout: Optimizing Layer Sparsity for Efficient LLM Training and Inference”

Layer dropout mostly disappeared from modern LLM pretraining because it was thought to hurt accuracy at scale.

But this Cerebras paper shows the opposite when configured correctly. 

They apply layer dropout at the whole Transformer-block level, sampled per sequence, use an increasing dropout distribution across depth, and a decreasing dropout schedule over training that decays to zero.

Across 2,400 runs up to 8.2B parameters, this saves up to 25% of training FLOPs while preserving accuracy, and makes models depth-elastic enough for early exit, layer skipping, and up to 1.55x faster self-speculative decoding.

https://t.co/TwjAJYdk7z

Follow @roupenmd for more balanced takes from an actual oncologist (and AI enthusiast) on where AI is at helping to treat cancer. 

Hyping a "cure" without understanding basic facts is disrespectful to all the patients and family members suffering from this disease. https://t.co/Ocrr84RpRm

This kind of tweet is both interesting and misleading.

On the one hand, who doesn’t want a personalized vaccine that treats their cancer and reduces the need for chemo?

On the other hand, there are many patients and families desperately looking for treatment. 

Presenting this as what cancer treatment looks like in 2026 is just not true:

1. Promising results in melanoma don’t mean personalized vaccines work across all cancers.

2. A treatment showing promise in a trial doesn’t mean most patients can get it or benefit from it.

I’d love to hear from oncologists like @RoupenMD @jasonwilliamsmd:
